transcript:
00:00 Ari (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we got about 55 minutes, we want to go deep on tail latency, p95/p99, streaming vs non-streaming, and your VPC/on-prem concerns. Introductions quick - uh Samir will drive the deep parts.
00:18 Maya (CTO): hey, thanks, Maya here, Diego, Priya, Alex on from infra. We've been seeing spikes in p99 around 350-600ms while p95 is fine ~120ms, so curious what's typical from Redwood and where to look.
00:35 Samir (SE): cool, thanks Maya. quick sanity check: these numbers are for your hosted calls through our API or from your Private VPC endpoint?
00:42 Maya: these are from our VPC peered instance, running a 13B open model quantized to 8-bit, mostly single-turn generation with streaming on for UI.
00:55 Samir: ok that's useful — streaming tends to increase p99 due to small write flushes and extra network hops. we'll unpack. first, quick overview of where tail comes from: model compute jitter, batching timeouts, KV cache misses, and network serialization/handshake.
01:12 Diego (Infra): can you explain batching timeouts? we thought batching was always reducing latency.
01:18 Samir: yes batching reduces average cost but if your workload has many small requests and we wait to fill a batch, we use a wait window or adaptive knobs. occasional slow requests or stragglers can hold up a batch or trigger small-batch execution which ups p99. Also mixing streaming with batching complicates things because partial tokens are flushed earlier.
01:36 Priya (ML Eng): our traffic pattern is chatty - many short messages then longer continuations. Could that cause small-batch effects?
01:43 Samir: definitely. chatty patterns with frequent short-turns cause a lot of small batches. Redwood runtime does continuous batching with dynamic thresholds, but tuning the max wait and preferred batch size helps. for p99, sometimes we increase the prefered batch size to reduce variance but that hurts p95 and median.
02:05 Alex (SRE): what about KV cache? we use a long conversation history, and when the cache misses we see big spikes.
02:11 Samir: KV cache misses are one of the top causes of tail spikes. two reasons: 1) cold cache loads require recomputing attention keys which increases compute, and 2) if cache is sharded across GPUs or nodes, cross-node fetches add network latency. for private deployments we recommend co-locating KV shards with workers or using a fast local HBM-backed cache.
02:36 Maya: our current KV is in-memory across two nodes with a small RDMA link, sometimes it degrades. is RDMA necessary?
02:42 Samir: RDMA helps for cross-node cache hot-paths, but it adds ops complexity. Alternately, pinning sessions to a worker (session affinity) reduces cross-shard misses at the cost of some load imbalance.
03:00 Ari: we have a small slide pack we'll send but Samir — can you talk about streaming vs non-streaming p99?
03:06 Samir: sure. streaming adds an additional write and flush per chunk, so network serialization happens more often; also TCP Nagle interactions or TLS record sizing can introduce microbursts. non-streaming pushes one larger response, so variability from network is smaller but you lose perceived latency improvements for first tokens. streaming helps perceived latency but can worsen p99 significantly if the network path has jitter.
03:28 Priya: hmm we see first-token fast but tails bad, that fits. any config changes to help?
03:33 Samir: options: 1) adjust chunk size and flush frequency for streaming, 2) enable adaptive flush that coalesces small chunks under load, 3) prefer server-side batching for the final tokens. we can also use keepalive/TCP tuning and TLS session reuse to reduce handshake jitter.
03:58 Diego: network hops — our VPC has a NAT gateway and private peering to Redwood, sometimes traffic routes through a transit gateway. how much does that add?
04:06 Samir: every hop can add 1-10ms at best, but bursty queues or NAT gateway cold pathing (first flow set up) can add 50-100ms. we usually advise direct VPC peering with pinned routes and avoid per-request NAT when possible. Also ensure ENI and c5n-like instances with jumbo frames if you can.
04:27 Alex: we use TLS termination on our gateway and then mTLS to Redwood — could double encrypt increase p99?
04:34 Samir: double TLS adds CPU on the gateway and extra context switches; if your gateway is CPU-constrained it can be a cause. use offload (TLS acceleration) or move termination closer to the worker for the hot path.
04:50 Maya: about quantization — we run int8 for cost. does quantization increase variance?
04:56 Samir: quantization usually reduces compute, but inference kernels can exhibit more variance if mixed-precision fallbacks occur or if dequant/decode paths touch slower memory. e.g., int8 kernels on some GPUs use specialized paths; if kernels are swapped at runtime due to sequence-length variance you can see spikes. also lower-precision may mean less opportunity for KV cache reuse if representations change slightly — in practice uncommon but possible.
05:24 Priya: any metrics we should log to correlate p99 with these causes?
05:29 Samir: yes: per-request batch size, batch wait time, KV cache hit/miss, shard location, kernel selection, GPU SM utilization, memcopy times, network RTT per hop, TLS handshake count, and streaming flush latency. we can provide a trace template.
05:50 Ari: Samir — can you walk through a real example trace and annotation?
05:55 Samir: yep, I'll share a contrived trace: 1) request arrives, session affinity hit? yes/no - 2) request queued 12ms for batching - 3) batch dispatched, queueing jitter 120ms due to straggler - 4) model kernel load 8ms, compute 40ms - 5) KV cache miss causes extra 85ms to fetch cross-node - 6) network egress to client 30ms - total ~295ms with most from cross-node KV and queueing jitter. bad-case p99 adds additional 200-300ms.
06:30 Maya: wow that matches our 350-600ms numbers.
06:35 Samir: some mitigations we discussed: session pinning, proactive prewarm of kernels, increase small-batch eviction thresholds, co-locate KV, change streaming flush behavior, and network path fixes. We'll propose a prioritized plan after reviewing your traces.
06:52 Diego: for on-prem, what are the recommendations? we might want Redwood private installed but we still have VLANs and Firewall rules.
06:59 Samir: private on-prem: 1) co-locate control and data plane inside your L2 where possible, 2) ensure low-latency interconnect (InfiniBand/RDMA) for KV cross-node, 3) use local KMS for keys to avoid network hops, 4) use pinned NICs for HBM access paths. we also recommend a canary worker rollout and shard-aware autoscaling to avoid cold-start spikes.
07:30 Jordan (PM): what's the difference in p99 guarantees between hosted, dedicated, and private?
07:36 Ari: hosted is best-effort with generally tight medians but less deterministic p99 under noisy neighbors, dedicated gives better capacity isolation and predictable throughput, private gives you full control and lowest network variability but requires you to follow infra best practices. with dedicated we can commit to lower p99 bounds with SLAs.
07:57 Maya: do you have any quick wins we can try in our staging before pilot?
08:02 Samir: yes: 1) switch streaming chunk size from 1 token flush to 32 tokens under load, 2) enable session affinity for 70% of traffic, 3) increase batch wait cap from 20ms to 40ms for batching sensitive endpoints, 4) deploy a lightweight KV pinning shim. we can provide config patches.
08:26 Priya: if we increase batch wait cap won't median get worse?
08:30 Samir: it might slightly increase median for single-turn requests, tradeoff is fewer small-batch executions and lower p99. We'll show the delta with benchmarks.
08:41 Alex: what about telemetry — we need per-token breakdown in traces.
08:45 Samir: we can send Redwood runtime traces that break down time into queuing, batch wait, kernel compute, memcopy, kv fetch, network egress. we recommend sample rate 1% for production and 100% for a short 1k run.
09:02 Ari: ok let's go into a few deeper notes on KV sharding — Samir take it away.
09:06 Samir: KV sharding strategies: hash-shard by session id to keep affinity, or LRU per-worker for memory efficiency. cross-shard fetches cost you in latency. for p99 you want deterministic placement; unpredictable eviction patterns create variance. for POC we recommend fixed session-to-worker mapping and periodic rebalancing during low-traffic windows.
09:36 Priya: how do you handle long conversations where one session becomes huge?
09:40 Samir: long histories we summarize or store a compressed keyset; also use recency windows for KV to bound memory. you can tier cold history to slower storage and bring it back under heavy access. that will add predictable latency when cold, which is preferable to random p99 spikes.
10:01 Maya: kernel selection — sometimes we see GPU kernel fallback logs and then latency spikes. is that expected?
10:08 Samir: yes if sequence lengths vary or memory pressure forces a fallback kernel. pre-compiling kernels for expected seq ranges and prewarming reduces this. Redwood's runtime can compile ahead-of-time for common lengths. for variable-length workloads, adaptive kernel selection with prewarm pools helps.
10:31 Diego: do you have recommendations for network MTU or NIC settings?
10:35 Samir: increase MTU to 9000 if supported, enable TCP keepalive, tune socket buffers, and prefer long-lived connections. also ensure your NAT/gateway isn't cycling ports aggressively.
10:48 Alex: curious about TLS overhead and mTLS — any instrumentation we can add?
10:52 Samir: log TLS handshakes per minute, CPU per gateway host, session reuse rate. if handshake rate is high you need connection pooling or an ALB with keepalive and TLS offload.
11:08 Priya: any notes about profiling GPUs for memcopy vs compute?
11:12 Samir: memcopy often dominates when KV fetches move lots of embeddings. profile memcpy latency, check PCIe vs NVLink transfer times, and track SM utilization. if memcopy > 30% of time you'll see weak scaling and variance.
11:30 Maya: can Redwood run a short benchmark against our VPC peering to reproduce p99?
11:34 Ari: yes we can. we propose 1k requests with your representative traffic (streaming on) and compare hosted vs private worker within your VPC. we'll also capture raw traces.
11:46 Diego: what about compliance/security — if we co-locate KV, keys, etc. how are they managed?
11:51 Samir: Redwood private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs; for pilot we can use our control plane with strict egress rules or a private control plane. we'll include SOC2 docs.
12:06 Jordan: recap and timeline?
12:09 Ari: recap: Redwood will share benchmark deck and trace template (Samir) by 11/17; Pioneer provides sample traffic and network diagram by 11/19; run a 1k benchmark in staging by 11/22; follow-up pilot kick-off 11/29.
12:29 Maya: sounds good. thanks everyone.
12:32 Ari: thanks all — I'll email notes and next steps.
12:40 (call ends)
